papers.title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure.
papers.abstract: Changes in oscillatory neural dynamics reflect-but may not necessarily determine-transitions between sleep stages and variations in sleep pressure. Here we show that sleep-control neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila (dFBNs) produce slow-wave activity (SWA) that is causally linked to sleep. The dFBN ensemble contains bistable cells whose membrane voltages oscillate between hyperpolarized DOWN and depolarized UP states. The oscillations rely on interhemispheric competition of two half-centers connected by inhibitory glutamatergic synapses. dFBN-restricted interference with glutamate release disrupts SWA and baseline as well as rebound sleep, whereas the optogenetic replay of SWA induces sleep. dFBNs generate SWA throughout the sleep-wake cycle (despite mutual antagonism with arousing dopaminergic neurons) and adjust its power to sleep need via sleep history-dependent increases in excitability and homeostatic synaptic depression. The oscillatory format permits a continuous encoding of sleep pressure but requires mechanisms that convert the amplitude-modulated signal into binary sleep-wake states.

papers.title: Recovery sleep induces analgesia via sleep ensembles of the zona incerta acting through distinct neural circuits in mice.
papers.abstract: Recovery sleep alleviates pain in humans, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identify a population of sleep-activated neuronal ensembles within the zona incerta (ZI) that mediate both non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and analgesia. Optrode recordings revealed preferential activity of these sleep ensembles during NREM sleep, whereas chronic pain markedly attenuated their activity. Activation of these ensembles increased NREM sleep and reduced pain sensitivity, whereas their inhibition reversed these effects. Gene profiling revealed enriched expression of neurotensin (NTS) within these neurons, and NTS knockdown significantly blunted their sleep-promoting and analgesic functions. Furthermore, ZI sleep ensembles project divergently to the lateral hypothalamus (LH) and the posterior thalamic nucleus (PO). ZI NTS projections to the LH specifically regulate NREM sleep without affecting nociception, whereas projections to the PO selectively mediate analgesia without impacting sleep. Collectively, these findings reveal that ZI sleep ensembles mediate recovery-sleep-induced analgesia, achieving modality specificity through segregated downstream targets.

papers.title: Disease progression shapes circadian and locomotor disruption in a model of multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system featuring a wide range of debilitating symptoms. Wearable activity recording devices have recently been adopted to improve symptom monitoring in MS, capturing symptoms related to sleep/wake cycles, circadian disruption, and fatigue. However, comparable measures of activity have yet been established in pre-clinical models of MS, the most widely used being experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). We therefore sought to characterize changes in continual home-cage activity over the course of EAE, and establish whether home-cage monitoring can be used as an observer-independent measure of disease progression. Our results showed that locomotor activity in the mid-active/dark phase was most severely affected by EAE. Disrupted circadian (24-hour) activity was observed during the peak and onset stages of disease. Bout activity analysis revealed >40-minute long activity bouts as a sensitive indicator of non-motor symptoms independent of clinical score-based motor deficits. Current assessment of disease progression in EAE relies on clinical scores, which primarily assess motor deficits through visual observation prone to observer bias. Various computed activity parameters were found to be altered during key disease stages, suggesting that a combination of activity measures can serve as objective indicators of disease progression. Overall, our results show that home-cage activity effectively captures signs of non-motor symptoms in the EAE model of MS and can serve as an observer-independent measure of EAE disease progression.

papers.title: Recombinant bovine αs1-casein ameliorates PCPA-induced insomnia-like behavioral and physiological abnormalities in mice.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a multifactorial sleep-wake disorder associated with altered neurotransmitter homeostasis, systemic inflammatory changes, and gut microbial dysbiosis. Recombinant bovine αs1-casein (RC) is a scalable milk-protein ingredient, but its effects on insomnia-like physiological and behavioral abnormalities have not been systematically evaluated. We investigated RC in a p-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA)-induced mouse model. Male ICR mice received RC (100, 300, or 500 mg kg-1 day-1), melatonin, Naoxinshu oral liquid, natural casein, or vehicle for 7 days after PCPA modeling. Body weight, open-field behavior, serum cytokines, brain neurotransmitters, hippocampal histology, organ indices, and cecal microbiota were assessed. RC improved body-weight recovery and open-field performance without altering major-organ indices. It increased brain 5-HT, 5-HIAA, dopamine, GABA, and glutamate concentrations and reduced the elevated norepinephrine concentration. High-dose RC reduced serum IL-6 and was associated with better-preserved hippocampal morphology. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed RC-associated changes in bacterial richness and community structure. The parallel physiological, neurochemical, inflammatory, and microbial changes support an association between RC administration and improvement of PCPA-induced insomnia-like abnormalities. These results identify recombinant bovine αs1-casein as a promising food-derived ingredient for further investigation in sleep-health applications, while the microbiota-gut-brain axis is presented as a testable mechanistic framework rather than a demonstrated causal pathway.

papers.title: Modulating Sleep Oscillations Through Targeted Memory Reactivation: Linking Functional Dynamics to Brain Microstructure
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation reputedly rely on the coordinated activity of sleep oscillations, which may facilitate the reactivation and redistribution of newly acquired memories. Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) during sleep can experimentally modulate these processes, although effects remain variable. Moreover, how learning-related microstructural plasticity relates to sleep oscillatory activity and spindle-related network dynamics remains poorly understood. We investigated whether auditory TMR modulates sleep spindles, slow oscillations (SOs) and their co-occurrence, whether these changes relate to motor memory consolidation and diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures of brain microstructure, and whether learning and TMR alter the evolution of cortico-cortical connectivity during spindle development. Methods: Sixty healthy young adults underwent five dMRI sessions before and after motor sequence learning (Day 1), after a post-training night of regular sleep (RS) or TMR (Day 2), and before and after relearning (Day 5). Baseline and experimental nights were recorded with 256-channel high-density EEG. Oscillation densities were analyzed using mixed-design ANOVAs and related to behavioral and dMRI changes using Pearson or Spearman correlations. Intra-spindle connectivity between 148 source-reconstructed cortical regions was compared between spindle onset and end, across nights and between groups using Network-Based Statistics. Results: Spindle density, SO density and SO-spindle co-occurrence remained stable across nights in the RS group but decreased after TMR. Higher spindle density and co-occurrence were associated with greater overnight performance gains, and all oscillatory measures were associated with learning-related dMRI changes in subcortical regions, notably striatum and thalamus. Connectivity increased from the beginning to the end of the spindle duration during the baseline night in both groups, but during the experimental night only in the RS group. Conclusions: Motor learning is associated with coordinated changes in sleep oscillatory activity, within-spindle cortical connectivity and brain microstructure, supporting a dynamic interaction between learning-induced plasticity and sleep-dependent network reorganization. Under the present stimulation conditions, TMR did not enhance these processes but instead reduced sleep oscillatory activity and attenuated spindle-related connectivity dynamics, underscoring the importance of precisely targeting endogenous sleep rhythms when using TMR.

Under the present stimulation conditions, TMR did not enhance motor memory consolidation but instead reduced sleep oscillatory activity and attenuated spindle-related connectivity dynamics.

papers.title: Slow Frontal Spindle Activity and Declarative Memory Retention During Daytime Naps.
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation refers to how newly encoded memories are strengthened and retained over time, and ample evidence indicates that sleep supports this process for both procedural and declarative memories. Although sleep spindles during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep have been associated with consolidation, it remains unclear whether all spindle types contribute equally. Spindles vary in frequency and topography, slow spindles (≤ 12.5 Hz) predominating frontally, fast spindles (> 12.5 Hz) parietally and recent work suggests that procedural memory consolidation relates to the temporal organization of spindles in 'trains' (events occurring < 6 s apart). We investigated whether a similar mechanism operates for declarative memory during daytime naps. Participants (Nap, N = 23; No-Nap, N = 15) completed an object-location task involving 36 item-location associations, tested immediately after learning and again following a 90-min nap opportunity or an equivalent wake period. The Nap group exhibited significantly better delayed memory, measured by combined recall-associative recognition scores and a greater proportion of nappers maintained or improved performance. Within the Nap group, memory was positively associated with local spindle density at frontal and parietal sites and with the proportion of slow frontal spindles clustered in trains during NREM2. Contrary to our expectations, however, these associations did not reach significance under two-tailed testing, possibly reflecting the limited sample size and thus lack of statistical power for an experimental design based on naps. Together, our results demonstrate a robust behavioural benefit of daytime naps for declarative memory retention and, more tentatively, point to slow frontal spindle activity as a candidate correlate for future work.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Chronic Intermittent Hypoxia Induces Persistent Venous Narrowing of Downstream Parenchymal Microvessels and Pial Veins in the Male Mouse Cortex.
papers.abstract: Chronic intermittent hypoxia (IH), a hallmark of sleep apnea, can lead to cerebral hypoperfusion and cognitive decline, though its precise impact on cerebral microcirculation remains unclear. This study investigated the longitudinal effects of 2-week chronic IH (8% O2, 6.5-min cycle for 6 hours/day) on brain microcirculation in the male mouse cortex. We observed a significant reduction in the diameters of pial veins (from 55 to 46 μm) and parenchymal venules (from 9.9 to 8.2 μm) after chronic IH relative to pre-IH conditions, while upstream arteries (47 to 44 μm) and arterioles (12.4 to 12.0 μm) were unaffected. This selective reduction in downstream venule diameter led to a significant increase in arterio-venous transit time, indicating reduced cerebral blood perfusion. Furthermore, neurovascular coupling (NVC) responses showed a substantial decrease, pointing to impaired microvascular function. Crucially, these neurovascular impairments were reversed by daily administration of an endothelin receptor antagonist during IH exposure, with the exception of pial vein constriction. In conclusion, reduced cerebral perfusion after chronic IH is associated with persistent narrowing of parenchymal venules and pial veins. These findings provide new insights into the cerebral microvascular complications of chronic IH and suggest the potential utility of neurovascular protective agents.

papers.title: Vigilance profiles at sleep onset in patients with difficulty initiating sleep, with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: Difficulty initiating sleep (DIS) is a core insomnia complaint, frequently associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms, yet its objective correlates remain elusive. Insomnia subtypes were merged into a single diagnosis in DSM-5 and ICSD-3 because their criteria lacked reliability, leaving open whether objective markers could help characterize insomnia heterogeneity. Conventional polysomnography (PSG) reduces the wake-sleep transition to a single 30-s epoch. We combined conventional and continuous EEG-based vigilance markers to characterize sleep onset in patients with and without a DIS complaint, and in patients with DIS with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed PSG recordings from 2,952 sleep-clinic patients, grouped by the self-reported complaint of difficulty falling asleep (Insomnia Severity Index item 1 [≥] 2: DIS, n = 1,328; no DIS, n = 1,624). In unmedicated patients with DIS (n = 556), depressive (BDI-II [≥] 14) and anxiety (STAI-T [≥] 45) symptoms were assessed. Vigilance was quantified on 3-s epochs with an intrinsic Vigilance Score (iVS), a probability-of-wakefulness index calibrated on each participant's own scored night, alongside the theta/alpha ratio and micro-sleep detection, and on 30-s epochs with automated hypnodensities. Results: Patients with DIS showed a longer sleep latency and slightly higher vigilance markers during both wakefulness and sleep, whereas the duration of the SOP itself was only marginally different (median 11.5 min in both groups). Deep sleep also accumulated later across the night (hypnodensity). In wakefulness preceding sleep onset, higher vigilance coexisted with more frequent brief vigilance drops. Among patients with DIS, depressive symptoms were associated with a less wake-like sleep-onset period despite more severe insomnia complaints, a finding not explained by differences in wake amount and convergent with hypnodensity. Anxiety symptoms showed a similar but weaker, non-significant pattern. Conclusions: In patients complaining of difficulty initiating sleep, the delay lies mainly before the first sleep epoch: once it is reached, progression to consolidated sleep is only marginally delayed, although its vigilance content may differ. Continuous EEG markers detect such differences, which are not captured by sleep staging. The association of depressive symptoms with a less vigilant sleep onset, despite worse complaints, suggests that similar insomnia complaints may rest on partly different physiological substrates, and that continuous vigilance markers could help revisit insomnia heterogeneity.

papers.title: Frontal theta power prospectively associated with response inhibition.
papers.abstract: A proactive mechanism has been postulated to promote successful inhibition. Specifically, this mechanism is thought to operate before any action-demanding or countermanding event has occurred. In the current study, we investigated whether theta-range oscillatory power measured using electroencephalography (EEG) could reflect this mechanism in a sample of healthy individuals performing a stop-signal task. We tested whether frontal-midline (FM) theta power preceding failed versus successful stop trials predicts inhibition success. Results from two experiments demonstrate that FM theta is indeed higher preceding successful stopping events than failed ones. However, theta power turned out to be equally stronger preceding slow than fast, go trials, suggesting that proactive slowing could explain the association between theta and stop success. There was no correlation between the strength of the within-subject theta-stop-success association and the within-subject theta-RT association. In sum, group-average-level analysis suggests strong overlap between FM theta associated with proactive inhibition and proactive slowing, respectively, while at the same time there are dissociations in terms of individual differences. A further, unexpected, finding was that FM alpha power was specifically associated with proactive inhibition but not with slowing, and, relative to theta, peaked closer in time to the action-demanding event.

papers.title: Sleep EEG oscillations and synaptic plasticity in memory consolidation across NREM and REM sleep.
papers.abstract: Based on a synthesis of recent advances, this review elucidates the distinct yet synergistic roles of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation. During NREM sleep, cortical slow oscillations (SOs) establish a temporal framework by alternating between UP and DOWN states, facilitating cross-regional communication. SOs phase-couple with thalamic spindles to coordinate hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), thereby driving the reactivation and transfer of labile hippocampal memories to neocortical networks for long-term storage. Concurrent synaptic homeostasis optimises network efficiency through global downscaling while selectively strengthening memory-relevant connections. In REM sleep, theta oscillations synchronise limbic-prefrontal-hippocampal circuits, and ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) waves further integrate emotional and procedural memories. The cholinergically dominant, monoamine-depleted neurochemical milieu of REM sleep promotes dendritic spine remodelling and sparse neuronal reactivation, enabling affective decoupling and synaptic refinement. Despite progress, key challenges remain in understanding cross-frequency oscillatory coupling among slow oscillations, spindles, ripples and REM-specific rhythms, glial contributions and clinical translation. Future integration of high-density electrophysiology with computational approaches may yield mechanistic models and clinically relevant biomarkers for sleep-based cognitive monitoring and intervention.

papers.title: Sleep Deprivation Selectively Alters Cellular Stress Responses During Exercise in the Heat in Young and Older Males.
papers.abstract: Older adults are at heightened risk of heat-related morbidity, particularly in occupational settings where insufficient sleep and heat exposure commonly coincide. Autophagy and other proteostatic pathways are essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis during acute physiological stress; however, whether acute sleep deprivation modifies these responses during exercise-heat stress remains unknown. Ten young (23±3 years) and 10 older (61±4 years) males completed an exercise-heat stress test following normal sleep and after 24 h of total sleep deprivation in which participants performed three 30-min cycling bouts at fixed rates of metabolic heat production (150, 200, and 250 W·m -2), each separated by 15 min rest in the heat (40°C, ~13% relative humidity). Autophagy and related cellular stress pathways were assessed before and after exercise. Sleep deprivation did not alter macroautophagy-related proteins, including LC3-II, the LC3-II/I ratio, ULK1 phosphorylation, or beclin-2 in either age group. However, p62 was reduced at end-exercise in young males following sleep deprivation (p=0.010), whereas the corresponding reduction in older males did not reach statistical significance. Sleep deprivation differentially altered proteins involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy, with LAMP-2A decreasing in young males but increasing in older males (both, p≤0.004). In older males, sleep deprivation reduced HSP90 and increased cleaved-caspase-3 and TNF-α (both, p≤0.048), indicating greater apoptotic and inflammatory signaling. Our findings indicate that 24 h of sleep deprivation does not broadly alter markers of macroautophagy during exercise-heat stress but selectively modifies cellular stress pathways in older males, with distinct responses observed in young and older males.

papers.title: Abnormal resting-state EEG microstates correlate with objective sleep parameters in insomnia disorder.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a common sleep disorder, and Electroencephalogram (EEG) microstates, which mirror transient cerebral cortical functional activity, are linked to sleep disorder pathophysiology. The microstate characteristics in insomnia patients and correlations with objective sleep parameters remain to be further explored. This study enrolled 45 insomnia disorder (ID) patients and 48 healthy controls (HC), collecting awake resting-state EEG for microstate analysis; 27 ID and 13 H C participants additionally completed overnight polysomnography (PSG), and exploratory correlation analyses of microstate and PSG data performed for the ID group. Compared with HC, ID patients had markedly shorter duration of microstate A and B, higher occurrence and contribution of microstate C, and reduced duration, occurrence and contribution of microstate D (p < 0.05). ID patients also showed significantly lower transition probabilities of A→D, B→D, D→A and D→B (p < 0.01), and higher probabilities of A→C, B→C, C→A and C→B (p < 0.05). Correlation analyses revealed that in the ID, microstate D occurrence was negatively correlated with rapid eye movement sleep proportion (REM Sleep%, r = -0.427, p = 0.026) and positively correlated with non-rapid eye movement sleep stage 1 proportion (S1%, r = 0.385, p = 0.047). ID patients present significant abnormalities in EEG microstates, and the occurrence of microstate D is correlated with objective sleep indicators of PSG. These findings suggest that EEG microstate parameters may reflect abnormalities in the sleep architecture of ID and may provide references for analyzing the cortical hyperarousal mechanism of chronic insomnia, constructing objective assessment schemes, and developing targeted neuroregulation interventions.

papers.title: Tracking Vigilance While Driving: Pilot Study of Heart Rate Variability Classification Under a Controlled Sleep-Deprivation Protocol.
papers.abstract: Decreased vigilance associated with drowsiness is a major cause of motor vehicle crashes, but its physiological characterization and detection remain difficult due to behavioral and environmental confounding factors. This study presents an original experimental framework combining a highly controlled sleep-deprivation protocol, repeated driving simulations, and a machine-learning-based heart rate variability (HRV) analysis to study the physiological and behavioral changes in vigilance during a prolonged period of wakefulness while driving. Twelve healthy young adults participated in a 30-h sleep-deprivation constant routine protocol that included driving simulations every two hours, with data collection: electrocardiography (ECG), subjective ratings of drowsiness, psychomotor vigilance test, and driving performance. The collected data was separated into two clearly identifiable vigilance states, a "Rested" and a "Tired" state, respectively, for the first and last driving sessions, of the protocol. Heart rate variability (HRV) features were extracted from ECG recordings, statistically analyzed, and submitted into supervised machine learning classifiers using participant-independent validation to assess their ability to distinguish between two experimentally defined states of vigilance. The accuracy of state separation was verified based on significant alterations observed in drowsiness ratings and psychomotor performance in the Tired compared to the Rested state. The variability in driving behavior, an indicator of impaired driving ability, increased significantly from the Rested compared to the Tired state. Several HRV features revealed significant differences between Rested and Tired states, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to large, observed for several metrics. Participant-independent machine learning analysis, namely Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation (LOSO-CV), showed that HRV metrics enable reliable discrimination between vigilance states, with all classifiers evaluated achieving average accuracy greater than 85%. This pilot study demonstrated that the proposed experimental framework, by reducing the major behavioral and environmental confounding factors, can generate two distinct states of vigilance at the physiological and behavioral levels, enabling reliable separation of experimental data, independent of any additional ground truths. The states separated by the framework enable the detection of decreased driving performance and efficiently label HRV data for vigilance classification. Nevertheless, the findings should be interpreted within the context of a pilot study conducted with a small cohort of healthy young adults.

papers.title: Clockophagy in Alzheimer's Disease: An Emerging Hypothesis Linking Circadian Dysfunction to Ferroptotic Vulnerability.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is frequently associated with sleep disturbances and circadian dysfunction, which may precede or accompany clinical manifestations and have been associated with amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology, tau abnormalities, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal vulnerability. Increasing evidence suggests that circadian regulation intersects with multiple cellular processes implicated in AD pathogenesis, including autophagy and ferroptosis. Among these mechanisms, clockophagy, an SQSTM1/p62-mediated selective autophagic process involved in BMAL1 degradation, has recently emerged as a potential molecular link between circadian regulation and cellular stress responses. In this review, we summarize current evidence connecting sleep disruption, circadian dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptotic susceptibility in AD, while highlighting the current limitations of mechanistic evidence. We further discuss the molecular basis of clockophagy and its potential relationship with BMAL1 regulation, oxidative lipid damage, and ferroptosis. Collectively, clockophagy is currently viewed as an emerging hypothesis that may contribute to AD-related pathological processes. Finally, we discuss potential therapeutic implications, including approaches targeting sleep and circadian organization, BMAL1-associated regulatory pathways, and lipid oxidative stress. Further studies are required to determine whether modulation of clockophagy can influence AD-related neurodegenerative processes.

papers.title: Frequent involvement of cingulate and insulo-opercular regions in sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy: A multimodal presurgical study.
papers.abstract: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is classically considered a frontal lobe epilepsy; however, accumulating evidence suggests that hypermotor seizures may arise from multiple frontal and extrafrontal regions. We characterized the anatomical distribution of best available localizations in patients with SHE using multimodal presurgical data. We retrospectively analyzed 17 patients with clinically diagnosed SHE who underwent comprehensive evaluation, including long-term video-electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring, 3-T high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, and, where indicated, magnetoencephalography, stereo-EEG (SEEG), and surgical assessment. Best available anatomical localizations were assigned using a hierarchical multimodal framework incorporating surgical, SEEG, and concordant noninvasive findings. Their anatomical distribution was subsequently assessed at the cohort level. Sixteen patients (94.1%) had an assigned best available localization. Cingulate or insulo-opercular regions were involved in 11 of 16 patients (68.8%), whereas the remaining cases were localized to other frontal regions. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 10 patients with SEEG-defined and/or surgically supported localizations, six involved cingulate or insulo-opercular regions. All patients were MRI-negative. In contrast, MRI-positron emission tomography fusion provided regionally informative anatomical findings in 16 of 17 cases and contributed to multimodal localization. Interictal epileptiform discharges were identified in 15 patients, whereas regionally informative ictal scalp EEG patterns were observed in eight; ictal interpretation was frequently limited by rapid propagation, movement-related artifacts, and delayed EEG onset. Focal cortical dysplasia-related histopathological findings were identified in five of seven resected specimens, whereas interpretation in two was limited by prior thermocoagulation. These descriptive findings indicate that cingulate and insulo-opercular regions were frequently represented among the identified localizations in this presurgical cohort. Multimodal evaluation integrating electroclinical, imaging, and invasive findings may support presurgical localization in MRI-negative SHE.

papers.title: Automation in sleep state classification and maturity evaluation of EEG in preterm-born infants.
papers.abstract: There is a growing need to automate EEG monitoring of preterm-born infants, particularly where expert evaluation is limited. However, existing models necessitate human intervention for comprehensive assessment, thereby limiting the clinical applicability. We collected 165 EEG records from 65 preterm-born infants. 8-channel EEG records were segmented every 30second and allocated into eight classes (three preterm-equivalent, four term-equivalent, and one noise class). We performed noise detection, sleep state classification, and maturity assessment through the classification. ImageNet pretrained ResNet-50 was finetuned to classify the segmented EEG images. A novel index, named "maturity rate," was calculated as the proportion of term-equivalent labels in each EEG recording. The model achieved a macro F1 score of 0.58 and Cohen's Kappa of 0.58 for the 8-class classification. When the labels were merged into active sleep, quiet sleep, and noise categories, performance improved to an F1 score of 0.84 and Kappa of 0.74. The maturity rate increased continuously with postmenstrual age at the time of recording, reflecting functional brain development beyond the term-preterm dichotomy. Our model enables end-to-end EEG assessment of sleeping newborns by simultaneously performing noise detection, sleep state classification, and maturity assessment, with minimal need for human intervention.

papers.title: Salivary Dim-Light Melatonin Onset is Associated with Functional Decline, Respiratory Symptom Emergence, and Survival in Early Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Sleep-wake and circadian disturbances are increasingly recognized in people living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (plwALS), but endogenous circadian phase timing and its prognostic significance in early disease remain unclear. We assessed whether salivary dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), an objective marker of central circadian phase, is altered in early plwALS and whether it provides prognostic information. In this prospective longitudinal observational study, plwALS within 18 months of symptom onset underwent home-based salivary melatonin sampling under dim-light conditions at 6 predefined time points around habitual sleep onset. Melatonin profiles were modeled using cubic smoothing splines, and DLMO was defined when the fitted curve first reached 3 pg/ml. Clinical, respiratory, and sleep assessments were collected at baseline (T0) and after 6 months (T6); a subgroup repeated saliva sampling at T6. Age- and sex-matched controls underwent melatonin profiling. Associations with disease progression, incident respiratory symptoms, and survival/tracheostomy were examined using regressions and survival analyses. A total of 50 plwALS were enrolled. Compared with controls, plwALS showed an earlier DLMO (20:24 ± 1:18 vs 20:58 ± 0:50; p = 0.028) despite similar habitual sleep onset and chronotype. Within ALS cohort, a later baseline DLMO correlated with worse functional/motor status, faster progression of disease, incident dyspnea/orthopnea by T6 (adjusted OR 3.11; p = 0.019), and poorer survival/tracheostomy-free outcome. In the resampled subgroup (n = 28), DLMO and melatonin-derived metrics did not change over ~6 months. Circadian phase alterations are detectable in early ALS. Baseline DLMO showed exploratory associations with functional, respiratory, and survival outcomes. Larger independent cohorts are required before DLMO can be considered a validated prognostic biomarker. ANN NEUROL 2026.

papers.title: Scalp EEG and Intrinsic Optical Signal Imaging for Noninvasive Detection of Spreading Depolarizations in the Rat Cortex.
papers.abstract: Spreading depolarization (SD) is a slowly propagating wave of massive neuronal and glial depolarization in the cerebral cortex that occurs in various brain diseases. However, noninvasive SD detection remains challenging. Here, we used scalp EEG and intrinsic optical signal (IOS) recordings in rats of both sexes to assess the feasibility of noninvasively detecting high-potassium-induced SDs in the cortex. Scalp EEG failed to detect DC-shifts but revealed a characteristic SD-related depression of AC-EEG activity, while concurrent infrared IOS recordings captured reliable SD-associated signals. Although the magnitudes of AC-EEG depression and IOS signals during scalp recordings were several times smaller than those recorded epidurally, both techniques enabled high-fidelity SD detection. These findings demonstrate that noninvasive monitoring of scalp EEG and infrared IOS imaging reliably detects SDs in the rat cerebral cortex.

papers.title: Cannabinoids and sleep bruxism: mechanistic rationale, polysomnographic evidence, and future research directions.
papers.abstract: Sleep bruxism (SB) is masticatory muscle activity during sleep, most often studied through its polysomnographic marker, rhythmic masticatory muscle activity (RMMA). Cannabinoids have attracted interest for their analgesic, anxiolytic and sleep-modulating properties, but whether they influence SB, and whether such modulation would benefit patients, remains unclear. This review examines cannabidiol (CBD), tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabinol (CBN) in relation to sleep, arousal and masticatory muscle activity, and separates what has been demonstrated from what is inferred. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and Web of Science for records published between 1 January 2004 and 14 June 2026, with searches last run on 14 June 2026. Cannabinoid terms were crossed with sleep terms and with bruxism terms, and searched independently for mechanistic literature. Seminal earlier work was retrieved by hand-searching reference lists. Each source was classified by level and directness of evidence. Meta-analytic evidence indicates that cannabis administration at therapeutic doses does not consistently alter total sleep time, sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency or sleep staging. A randomised polysomnographic trial of CBN missed its primary endpoint (wake after sleep onset); in uncorrected secondary and tertiary analyses, 300 mg reduced the electroencephalographic arousal index and sleep onset latency and increased N2 sleep. Preclinical polysomnography supports a hypnotic action of CBN and of its brain-penetrant metabolite, with partial tolerance within two weeks. One randomised trial reported that topical CBD reduced a portable device bruxism index and masseter activity in patients with SB and painful temporomandibular disorders, through a proposed local mechanism involving myorelaxation and analgesia. The entire direct clinical evidence base comes from a single research group, and no study has measured RMMA by polysomnography under any cannabinoid. Two distinct pathways could link cannabinoids to SB, one peripheral and one central, and neither has been demonstrated in patients with SB. The clinically relevant question is not whether a cannabinoid lowers a motor activity index, but whether it improves outcomes that matter in patients whose SB carries consequences. Trials combining polysomnography, masseter electromyography and patient-centred outcomes are required before any clinical recommendation. Not applicable (narrative review).

papers.title: Video EEG in pediatric epilepsy: Diagnostic significance and association between frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to compare video electroencephalogram (VEEG) and routine electroencephalogram (EEG) in childhood epilepsy diagnosis and analyze the correlation between EEG frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity. One hundred and sixty children suspected of having epilepsy underwent routine EEG and VEEG examinations. Diagnostic efficacy and detection rates were compared. Cognitive function was evaluated in 80 children diagnosed with epilepsy, who were allocated into normal intelligence (35 cases), borderline intelligence (25 cases), and intelligence-impaired (20 cases) groups. Clinical data, EEG parameters, and their correlation with cognitive impairment were analyzed. VEEG showed higher sensitivity, accuracy, and negative predictive value, and detection rates of epileptiform discharges, synchronous clinical seizures, and clinical symptoms than routine EEG (p < 0.05). Clinical characteristics and EEG parameters differed among the three groups (p < 0.05). The relative power of δ and θ bands and the awake and sleep discharge indices were positively correlated with cognitive impairment severity (r = 0.300, 0.643, 0.622, and 0.456), whereas α and β band power were negatively correlated (r = -0.515 and -0.410) (all p < 0.001). VEEG demonstrated higher diagnostic performance than routine EEG, and EEG frequency band power was correlated with cognitive impairment severity.

papers.title: Circadian disruption exacerbates alcohol-induced cardiac injury through impaired cellular quality control and increased cardiomyocyte death.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms orchestrate 24-h oscillations in physiology and gene expression in many tissues, including the heart. Disruptions to these rhythms have been linked to increased cardiovascular risk and impaired cellular homeostasis. However, the extent to which circadian disruption influences cardiac responses to environmental stressors such as alcohol, remains poorly understood. Herein, we performed RNA-sequencing and transcriptomic analysis on hearts from C57BL/6 J mice exposed to alcohol for ten weeks and collected at two distinct circadian time points (Zeitgeber Time (ZT)8 and ZT20). Principal component analysis and differential expression profiling revealed robust time-of-day-dependent transcriptional programs induced by alcohol, with significant enrichment of pathways governing mitochondrial quality control, autophagy/mitophagy, ferroptosis, and key signaling nodes (FOXO, MAPK, AMPK, mTOR, HIF, Hippo). To investigate the impact of circadian disruption, we compared alcohol-challenged hearts from circadian disrupted and control mice. Circadian disruption markedly altered transcriptional profiles and pathways associated with cardiomyopathy and insulin resistance, while further amplifying dysregulation of quality control and stress signaling networks. At the cellular level, alcohol exposure reduced autophagosome formation in isolated adult cardiomyocytes and this decrease was exacerbated by circadian disruption. Further, circadian disruption impaired mitochondrial quality control by reducing ATP production, altering mitophagy, and mitochondrial dynamics, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction. These alterations were accompanied by increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and elevated apoptotic cell death compared with either condition alone. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that circadian disruption exacerbates alcohol-induced molecular and cellular cardiac injury by compromising cellular quality control processes, mitochondrial integrity, and cell survival pathways. These findings identify mechanisms that may contribute to increased susceptibility to alcohol-induced cardiac dysfunction and may offer novel approaches to mitigate alcohol-related cardiac injury in shift-workers or individuals with disrupted circadian rhythms.

papers.title: Association of Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet with sleep quality and quantity, inflammation and oxidative stress in Iranian adults: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Although some studies have examined the relation of Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet with sleep disorders, their results were inconclusive and none of them considered inflammation and oxidative stress biomarkers as potential contributors. We evaluated the relation between MIND diet and sleep parameters in Iranian adults, taking biomarkers into account. A sample of 535 adults (46 % were female), with a mean age of 42·6 years, was selected via a multistage-cluster random sampling for this cross-sectional investigation. Dietary data were collected via a validated FFQ. Sleep quality and sleep duration were assessed by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index questionnaire. Concentration of biomarkers was assessed using participants' blood samples, taken after a period of night-fasting. In fully-adjusted model, participants in the highest (v. lowest) tertile of MIND diet had 54 % lower odds of short sleeping (ORT3v.T1 = 0·46, 95 % CI: 0·22-0·93), and subjects in the highest tertile of MIND score had 56 % lower odds of poor sleep quality (ORT3v.T1 = 0·44, 95 % CI: 0·21-0·95). These associations were stronger in participants with overweight and obesity. Higher adherence to MIND was associated with a lower probability of sleep disturbance (ORT3v.T1 = 0·27, 95 % CI: 0·08-0·89). There was no statistically significant association between the MIND diet and either oxidative stress or inflammatory biomarkers (P > 0·05). These findings highlighted inverse associations between higher MIND adherence and sleep disorders among Iranian adults. No significant associations between MIND adherence and biomarkers of inflammation and oxidative stress were found.

papers.title: Decoding user satisfaction during reading of pre-defined question-answer pairs: BCI approach using delta and gamma EEG.
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has intensified the need for robust evaluation frameworks to align artificial intelligence (AI) behavior with human expectations. While current reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) strategies heavily rely on explicit, post-hoc self-reports, these metrics are fundamentally limited by subjective biases and user non-compliance. To address this, the current study presents a novel brain-computer interface (BCI) framework that systematically characterizes the continuous, implicit neural correlates of user satisfaction and dissatisfaction during a reading-based evaluative task involving pre-validated LLM-generated question-answer pairs. Sixty-four-channel electroencephalography (EEG) data were recorded from 30 participants while they read and evaluated various LLM-generated responses. To capture genuine subjective experiences, individual trials were relabeled based on post-trial 5-point Likert scale ratings into five distinct evaluative states, and spatiotemporal spectral analyses were performed. A ShallowFBCSPNet architecture was further used to evaluate single-trial classification between the very satisfied and very dissatisfied conditions under a subject-mixed cross-validation scheme. Spatiotemporal spectral analyses revealed distinct neural oscillatory dynamics that temporally dissociate satisfaction and dissatisfaction. When reading highly satisfactory responses, a pronounced, sustained enhancement of low-frequency delta power was observed within the bilateral frontotemporal areas during the middle (4-8 s) and late (8-12 s) reading intervals, indexing high-order cognitive consolidation and reward processing. Conversely, processing highly dissatisfactory responses led to a localized suppression of high-frequency gamma power in the right frontotemporal region during the early interval (0-4 s), reflecting an immediate affective appraisal and expectation violation. Utilizing the ShallowFBCSPNet architecture, the system successfully discriminated between the "very satisfied" and "very dissatisfied" states, achieving an average accuracy of 81% under a subject-mixed cross-validation scheme. These findings demonstrate that user evaluative states are encoded via distinct frequency-specific cortical networks over differing temporal windows. By bridging cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, this study establishes the conceptual and empirical foundation for passive BCI-driven implicit feedback channels, laying groundwork toward future real-time paradigms for next-generation LLM alignment; the classification result should be interpreted as a feasibility demonstration rather than an estimate of real-world decoding accuracy.

papers.title: Cross-cohort transfer of clinical Alzheimer's EEG signatures to cognitively healthy APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 risk carriers using differentiable logic gate networks.
papers.abstract: Neural alterations associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) may emerge years before clinical diagnosis, and genetic risk factors such as APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 may identify individuals vulnerable to these shifts. We tested whether electroencephalography (EEG) signatures learned from clinically diagnosed AD patients transfer to cognitively healthy middle-aged adults carrying these variants. Differentiable logic gate networks (Diff-Logic) and neural baselines were trained on log-relative power spectral density features from a clinical cohort of AD patients and cognitively normal (CN) controls. These models were then applied without retraining to an independent genetic-risk cohort of neutral-risk non-carriers (N), APOE-ε4-only carriers (A+P-), and dual APOE-ε4/PICALM G-allele carriers (A+P+), yielding a continuous AD-like EEG signature score per participant. Diff-Logic matched neural baselines in clinical classification (balanced accuracy 0.809±0.028; AUROC 0.845±0.023) while enabling edge inference with a 7.4× model-size reduction and 0.22 ms model-only latency on a 7 W single-core CPU. In the genetic-risk cohort, scores were highest in A+P+ participants (0.393±0.167) relative to N (0.296±0.154) and A+P- (0.285±0.143; subject-level mean ± SD). This elevation was nominally significant before correction (A+P+ vs. A+P-, punc=0.036) but did not survive Holm correction (pHolm=0.109), and the cohort carried no AD pathology or conversion ground truth; the association was therefore exploratory. Integrated gradients attribution of the trained model showed genetic-risk relevance in delta, theta, and alpha, partially overlapping clinical AD topography. These findings support the feasibility of zero-shot EEG transfer in genetically at-risk individuals and highlight the need for replication in larger cohorts. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Shyamal-Dharia/ad-difflogic-transfer.

papers.title: Circadian Misalignment and Chrononutrition in Type 2 Diabetes: Mechanistic Insights and Translational Gaps.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate glucose metabolism, insulin secretion, hepatic glucose production, peripheral insulin sensitivity, nutrient handling, and energy balance. Observational studies have associated circadian timing disruption through shift work, irregular sleep, artificial light at night, social jet lag, late eating, or inconsistent meal timing with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). This narrative review integrates molecular, clinical, nutritional, and pharmacological evidence linking circadian misalignment with diabetes, with emphasis on chrononutrition, time-restricted eating, glucose variability, diabetes-related complications, melatonin/MTNR1B-related susceptibility, exogenous melatonin, continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), digital phenotyping, and chronopharmacology. A structured narrative literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies on circadian biology, diabetes, meal timing, time-restricted eating, melatonin signaling, MTNR1B, circadian biomarkers, CGM, and time-informed therapeutic strategies. Mechanistic and preclinical studies establish clock-metabolism coupling, whereas controlled human physiological studies support time-of-day variation in insulin secretion, postprandial responses, and glucose handling; diabetes-specific interventional and complication-outcome evidence remains limited. Chrononutrition and time-restricted eating may support glycemic regulation only as individualized adjuncts to standard diabetes care, not as replacements for established treatment; medication review and hypoglycemia monitoring are essential, particularly for patients using insulin or insulin secretagogues. Translation into routine care requires longer diabetes-specific trials, standardized outcomes, validated biomarkers, and patient-centered implementation protocols.

papers.title: Impact of Music as Environmental Enrichment on Chronic Stress and Anxiety-Related Responses in Broiler Chickens.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of classical music as auditory environmental enrichment on chronic stress and anxiety-related responses in broiler chickens. Two hundred Cobb 500 chicks were assigned to a control group (no enrichment) or an enriched group exposed to classical music for 6 h daily from 1 to 40 days of age. At 40 days, affective states were assessed using the attention bias test (ABT), while chronic stress was evaluated through feather corticosterone (CORT) concentrations. Music-exposed birds had significantly lower feather CORT concentrations than controls (p < 0.0001), indicating reduced chronic stress. No significant treatment effects were detected for ABT behavioral measures. However, music-exposed birds showed a numerically longer latency to take the first step (p = 0.055), although this difference did not reach statistical significance. Overall, these findings demonstrate that classical music enrichment can reduce physiological indicators of chronic stress in broilers, while evidence for effects on anxiety-related behavior remains inconclusive. The results suggest that auditory enrichment may help reduce chronic stress in broilers under the conditions evaluated and highlight the need for further replicated studies to clarify its effects on affective states and behavioral responses.

papers.title: Fear-EEG-AI: A Conceptual and Operational Framework for Designing EEG-AI Systems for the Inference of Fear-Compatible Neurophysiological States.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and artificial intelligence (AI) are central tools in affective computing, yet fear-related inference remains constrained by a gap between experimental performance and deployable evidence: high accuracy on controlled datasets guarantees neither neurobiological specificity, nor robustness across users, nor traceable inference. EEG does not measure fear directly; it captures cortical dynamics compatible with threat processing, arousal or vigilance. This paper introduces the Fear-EEG-AIFramework, a technology-independent architecture for designing, validating and deploying EEG-AI systems targeting fear-compatible neurophysiological states. Building on a prior systematic review, it organizes development into three hierarchical levels-neurobiological foundation, neuroelectric correlates and computational modeling-governed by six cross-cutting principles, and makes them evaluable through eight observable dimensions, the Fear-EEG-AI Alignment Index (FAI) and five validation evidence levels. Applied to the eight eligible studies of that corpus by two raters who had not drafted the instrument, with adjudication by a third, the rubric reached 67.2% exact agreement (quadratic-weighted κ=0.741; ICC(2,1) =0.744). Under 10,000 admissible weightings the equal-weight ordering survived in 10.1% of draws, and one of 56 ordered pairs met a stability criterion fixed before the pairwise results were tabulated. The index is therefore reported as a descriptor of methodological documentation and not as a ranking of implementations.

papers.title: Association between low-carbohydrate diet scores and macrovascular events or all-cause mortality in adults with type 1 diabetes in Japan.
papers.abstract: The effects of lifestyle factors on macrovascular events or all-cause mortality remain unclear in type 1 diabetes. We examined the associations of diet, physical activity, and sleep with these outcomes among adults with type 1 diabetes living in Japan. This multicenter prospective cohort included 352 adults with type 1 diabetes from the Juntendo-Aso Type 1 Diabetes cohort. Lifestyle factors were assessed by questionnaire. Dietary intake was evaluated using a brief-type self-administered diet history questionnaire, from which Total, Plant, and Animal low-carbohydrate diet scores were calculated. The primary composite outcome was the first occurrence of ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral artery disease, or all-cause mortality. Associations were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models. Mean age was 51.4 ± 15.1 years, mean HbA1c was 7.9 ± 1.1%, and carbohydrate accounted for 49.3% of energy intake. During follow-up, 35 participants experienced the primary composite outcome. In multivariable Cox models, the Total LCDS (HR, 0.90; 95% CI: 0.82-0.98; P = 0.012), Plant LCDS (HR, 0.85; 95% CI: 0.76-0.94; P = 0.003), and Animal LCDS (HR, 0.93; 95% CI: 0.87-0.996; P = 0.037) were inversely associated with the outcome. Among adults with type 1 diabetes living in Japan, low-carbohydrate dietary patterns, particularly the Plant low-carbohydrate diet score, were inversely associated with macrovascular events or all-cause mortality.

papers.title: Nutrition, Circadian Regulation, and the Gut-Melatonin-Visceral Adipose Tissue Axis: An Integrative Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) dysfunction is a major determinant of obesity-related metabolic disorders, including insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Growing evidence indicates that VAT function is regulated by a complex interplay between nutrition, circadian rhythms, intestinal melatonin secretion, and the gut microbiota rather than by isolated metabolic pathways. The gastrointestinal tract represents an important interface between dietary exposures, microbial activity, immune signaling, and host metabolic regulation. Melatonin is a potential component of this network because it participates in circadian regulation and has been detected in gastrointestinal tissues, while experimental studies suggest that intestinal melatonin signaling may interact with gut microbial and metabolic processes. However, the cellular sources, quantitative contribution, local dynamics, and physiological significance of intestinal melatonin remain incompletely established, particularly in humans. This narrative review integrates current evidence regarding the interactions between nutrition, circadian regulation, intestinal melatonin, gut microbiota, and visceral adipose tissue. Rather than proposing a validated causal pathway, we introduce the Gut-Melatonin-Visceral Adipose Tissue (Gut-Melatonin-VAT) Axis as an integrative, hypothesis-generating conceptual framework that organizes established interactions together with candidate mechanisms requiring further experimental validation. Particular attention is given to the bidirectional relationships among dietary composition, meal timing, microbial rhythmicity, intestinal signaling, immune regulation, and VAT dysfunction. The framework may provide a basis for generating testable hypotheses concerning nutritional, chrononutritional, microbiota-targeted, and melatonin-related interventions, while recognizing that direct human evidence validating the complete pathway is currently lacking.

papers.title: The influence of health conditions, lifestyle factors, and stress on seafarers' self-rated health - a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Self-rated health (SRH) is a validated holistic indicator of health, yet evidence among seafarers is limited. We examined how health conditions and lifestyle factors relate to poor SRH and whether perceived stress modifies these associations in active-duty seafarers. A total of 22,432 international seafarers who were on board were included in the analysis of an electronic survey distributed via 52 shipping and manning companies in February-March 2024. An 82-item questionnaire assessed SRH, self-reported health conditions, lifestyle factors (physical activity, sleep/feeling rested, smoking, alcohol risk, loneliness, screen time), and perceived stress. Cross-sectional analyses used descriptive statistics and logistic regression. Models were adjusted for age, sex, rank, and time on board; stress was added as an independent predictor. Additive interactions between stress and lifestyle factors were evaluated using relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI). Poor SRH was strongly associated with multimorbidity and selected conditions, particularly depression/anxiety, gastrointestinal issues, and musculoskeletal issues. In fully adjusted lifestyle models, sedentary behavior, not feeling rested, smoking, loneliness, and excess screen time remained associated with poor SRH, while alcohol risk was not. Stress was independently associated with poor SRH and amplified the effects of not feeling rested, loneliness, and excess screen time. Self-rated health captured a combined burden of physical and mental symptoms as well as recovery--related and psychosocial factors relevant to life at sea. The stress-sensitive clustering of poor sleep/rest, loneliness, and high screen time suggests that interventions may be most effective when stress management is integrated with fatigue and social-connection measures. Health conditions and modifiable lifestyle/psychosocial factors were associated with seafarers' SRH, and perceived stress acted as both an independent predictor and an effect modifier. Targeting sleep, stress, social well-being, and sedentary recovery patterns may improve perceived health and potentially safety on board.

papers.title: Perceptions of Intra-Operative EEG Brain Monitoring During Pediatric Anesthesia Among Children and Parents: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Survey.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring during pediatric anesthesia may improve perioperative safety by optimizing anesthetic titration and reducing adverse outcomes. However, little is known about patient and caregiver perceptions regarding this technology and its implementation into routine anesthesia care. This study evaluates perceived importance, utility, and extent of reassurance provided by intra-operative EEG monitoring among pediatric patients and their parents. Secondary aims include identifying concerns surrounding general anesthesia (GA), concerns surrounding EEG monitoring, cost and willingness to pay, and sociodemographic and medical factors shaping these attitudes. We conducted an exploratory cross-sectional survey at a tertiary pediatric hospital in Singapore between July 2022 and September 2025. Respondents were parents of children aged 1-18 years and children aged 12-18 scheduled for elective procedures under general anesthesia. A 16-item anonymized questionnaire assessed perceptions of intra-operative EEG monitoring, concerns about anesthesia, and attitudes regarding the cost of EEG monitoring. Of 400 respondents (100 children, 300 parents), 83.5% rated intra-operative brain monitoring as "very" or "quite" important and 93% reported feeling more reassured by its use. Children were most concerned about intraoperative awareness and failure to awaken, whereas parents were most concerned about anesthetic side effects and dosage. Parents with higher education and whose children had prior anesthetic exposure reported greater reassurance from EEG monitoring. Cost was the leading concern regarding EEG monitoring, particularly among parents from families residing in public housing. Despite this, most parents (75%) and children (59%) expressed willingness to pay for EEG monitoring. Pediatric patients and parents viewed intra-operative EEG monitoring as important and reassuring, and expressed willingness to support its implementation despite cost concerns. These findings suggest that families are unlikely to be a major barrier to EEG adoption and highlight the need for clinician- and system-level strategies to integrate EEG monitoring into family-centered pediatric anesthesia care.

papers.title: Surgical Success in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients Using Preoperative Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy and Awake Endoscopy Considering Disease Severity.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a prevalent disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of airway obstruction during sleep, leading to fragmented sleep and oxygen desaturation. Identifying the precise site and pattern of obstruction is essential for surgical success. Awake endoscopy with Müller's maneuver (AEMM) has long been used, but drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) offers dynamic assessment under sleep-like conditions. To retrospectively compare surgical outcomes of OSA patients evaluated with DISE versus AEMM, stratified by disease severity, and to determine whether the comparative value of DISE over AEMM differs according to OSA severity as measured by AEMM (AHI). Records of 102 OSA patients undergoing sleep surgery between January 2022 and December 2024 at Hamad Medical Corporation were reviewed. Patients were grouped into AEMM-only (n = 54) and DISE (n = 48). Surgical success was defined as postoperative AHI < 15 events/hour and at least 50% reduction from baseline. Statistical analysis included independent and paired t-tests, chi-square tests, and the Johnson-Neyman procedure to identify AHI-based thresholds of DISE benefit. DISE group had higher surgical success compared to AEMM (62.5% vs. 40.7%, p = 0.114). Preoperative and postoperative AHI changes were significant in both groups (p < 0.001). Stratification revealed that moderate-to-severe OSA patients (AHI > 16.7) had significantly better outcomes when surgery was based on DISE (p < 0.001). In patients with mild OSA (AHI < 16.7), DISE conferred no additional benefit over AEMM. DISE-based surgical planning improves outcomes in moderate-to-severe OSA, while AEMM remains adequate for mild OSA cases. Disease severity should guide the choice of preoperative airway assessment method.

papers.title: Folic Acid Oversupplementation Alters Global DNA Methylation and Circadian Clock Gene Expression in FaDu Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma Cells: An Exploratory Study.
papers.abstract: Folic acid (FA), the synthetic form of folate (vitamin B9), is a vitamin involved in one-carbon metabolism, DNA synthesis, and DNA methylation. Because folate metabolism influences methyl donor availability, FA availability may affect circadian clock gene regulation through methylation-related or other metabolic mechanisms in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). This exploratory study aims to determine whether FA oversupplementation influences cell viability and alters global DNA methylation, as well as the expression and methylation status of circadian clock genes in HNSCC cells. FaDu HNSCC cells were treated with 20 or 80 μM FA and compared with a no-added-FA (NF) reference condition. Cell viability was assessed using a CCK-8 assay after 48 and 72 h. For methylation and gene expression analyses, cells were synchronized with forskolin and treated with FA (20 or 80 μM) for 7 days. Global DNA methylation was measured using a 5-methylcytosine colorimetric assay. Following the NF and 80 μM FA treatment, cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) island methylation in the BMAL1 and PER2 promoters, RNA expression, and protein levels were analyzed by bisulfite conversion followed by Sanger sequencing, qPCR, and ELISA. FA treatment significantly reduced cell viability at 48 h (20 μM, p < 0.05; 80 μM, p < 0.01) and 72 h (both concentrations p < 0.01). Global DNA methylation was modestly reduced, reaching statistical significance only in the 80 μM FA group (p < 0.05). No qualitative differences were observed in the promoter methylation of the analyzed CpG regions of BMAL1 and PER2 following 80 μM FA treatment. However, BMAL1 and PER2 mRNA expressions were significantly increased (p < 0.05), while protein levels showed non-significant upward trends following 80 μM FA treatment. These exploratory findings suggest that the observed transcriptional changes are unlikely to be explained by methylation changes within the analyzed promoter regions of BMAL1 and PER2. The mechanisms underlying these changes remain unclear and require further investigation.

papers.title: Balancing Local and Global Dependencies in EEG Emotion Recognition via Multi-Scale Hybrid Attention.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based emotion recognition remains challenging due to the low signal-to-noise ratio, non-stationarity, strong inter-subject variability, and the distribution of affect-related information across multiple temporal resolutions. Although recent deep architectures have increasingly combined multi-scale local feature extraction with global dependency modeling, the adaptive integration of multi-scale representations before global encoding remains comparatively underexplored. To address this issue, we propose DSFConformer, an EEG emotion-recognition framework integrating multi-scale spatiotemporal convolution, Dynamic Sparse Feature Fusion (DSFF), and lightweight Transformer-based global modeling. The multi-scale encoder captures complementary local EEG dynamics at different temporal resolutions, while DSFF performs sample-adaptive feature reweighting and sparse suppression to reduce the influence of redundant or noise-sensitive responses. A Lite Transformer is subsequently employed to model global contextual dependencies with reduced computational cost. Experiments on the SEED dataset were conducted under complementary evaluation protocols. DSFConformer achieved an accuracy of 96.08% under chronological block-wise segment-level cross-validation. Under the stricter trial-wise protocol, it achieved 78.81% accuracy, statistically comparable to EEG-Conformer at 78.77%, with no significant paired difference. Ablation analyses further demonstrate that multi-scale convolution and DSFF provide the primary recognition-performance gains, whereas the Lite Transformer mainly improves computational efficiency while preserving comparable accuracy. Cross-session and leave-one-subject-out analyses further assess model robustness and generalization. Overall, the results indicate that adaptive sparse fusion of multi-scale EEG representations provides an effective approach for balancing local representation learning, noise-aware feature integration, and efficient global dependency modeling.

papers.title: Syndromic Autism in Helsmoortel-Van der Aa Syndrome: From Clinical Suspicion to Genetic Diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Syndromic autism refers to autism spectrum disorder (ASD) occurring as part of an identifiable genetic syndrome. Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome (HVDAS/ADNP syndrome) is a rare autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the ADNP gene. We report a 10-year-old boy with ASD and intellectual disability who exhibited delayed motor and language development, characteristic facial dysmorphism, early tooth eruption, endocrine abnormalities, electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities, and urogenital findings. Following unremarkable karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous pathogenic de novo frameshift variant, c.1239_1240del, p.(Gln414Valfs*25) in ADNP. This case emphasizes the importance of considering a syndromic etiology in children with ASD accompanied by developmental delay, dysmorphic features, neurological findings, or multisystem involvement, and supports comprehensive genetic evaluation when first-tier testing is unrevealing.

papers.title: Dynamic within-person associations between problematic social media use and sleep quality among university students: The mediating role of nomophobia and the moderating role of trait rumination.
papers.abstract: Problematic social media use (PSMU) and poor sleep quality are prevalent among university students. Although previous research has documented associations between PSMU and sleep problems, less is known about the short-term dynamic mechanisms underlying this relationship and the individual differences that may shape vulnerability. Drawing on intensive longitudinal data and dynamic structural equation modeling, this study examined a moderated mediation model in which nomophobia (i.e. anxiety or distress arising from being unable to access or use one's mobile phone) mediated the association between PSMU and poor sleep quality, with trait rumination examined as a moderator of this indirect association. A 21-day daily diary study was conducted with 228 Chinese university students. At the between-person level, higher PSMU was associated with greater nomophobia and poorer sleep quality. At the within-person level, increases in PSMU were prospectively associated with greater nomophobia, which subsequently predicted poorer sleep quality, supporting an indirect association through nomophobia. This indirect association was more pronounced among students with higher levels of trait rumination. By capturing dynamic day-to-day processes, these findings extend current understanding of how PSMU may contribute to poorer sleep during emerging adulthood and highlight nomophobia and rumination as potential targets for interventions aimed at promoting healthier digital habits and sleep.

papers.title: Six-month comparative outcomes of endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty versus laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy: an MBSAQIP analysis.
papers.abstract: North American data regarding long-term efficacy and durability of endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) are remarkably scarce outside of clinical trial settings hampering our understanding of its optimal role in the obesity care continuum. The aims of this study are to compare safety and efficacy of elective ESG versus laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) at 6 months using accredited MBSAQIP centers. Data were obtained from the Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Accreditation and Quality Improvement Program (MBSAQIP) database for 2023 and merged with the 6‑month follow‑up data file. The primary objectives of the study were to characterize the long-term six-month changes in weight and metabolic comorbidities of ESG patients in contrast to their LSG counterparts. Logistic regression models were to evaluate for differences in six-month serious complications and emergency department readmissions between ESG and LSG. A total of 115,476 patients were included, comprising 114,967 LSG and 509 ESG procedures. Patients undergoing ESG were slightly older (44.5 ± 11.2 vs. 42.4 ± 11.9 years, p = 0.0001) and had lower baseline BMI (40.9 ± 8.6 vs. 45.0 ± 7.8 kg/m2, p < 0.0001) and mean body weight (113.2 ± 28 vs. 124.5 ± 26.3 kg). At 6 months, LSG resulted in greater weight reduction, with larger BMI loss (8.2 ± 10.8 vs. 3.9 ± 12.0 kg/m2, p < 0.0001), and total weight loss (22.6 ± 35.6 vs. 11.1 ± 37.7 kg, p < 0.0001). For patients undergoing LSG, there was a near 50% reduction in medication/insulin-dependent diabetes along with improvements in rates of dyslipidemia, hypertension, and sleep apnea. Importantly, no clinically meaningful comorbidity improvements from baseline to 6 months were seen following ESG. When compared to ESG at 6 months, LSG provides an improvement in total body weight loss, has a reduced operative time, and is associated with dramatic metabolic comorbidity improvement including a reduction in resolution of medication and insulin-dependent diabetes. No clinically meaningful comorbidity resolution was seen in patients receiving ESG compared to LSG at 6 months although this cohort was less comorbid at baseline.

papers.title: Pharmacological Interventions for Acute Stress Disorder and for the Prevention and Treatment of Post-traumatic Stress Disorder in Children and Adolescents: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Traumatic events are common during childhood and adolescence and may lead to acute stress disorder (ASD) or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), both associated with developmental, cognitive and functional impairment. Although trauma-focused psychotherapies are recommended as first-line treatments, pharmacological interventions are frequently used in clinical practice despite limited evidence in paediatric populations. To review the evidence on pharmacological interventions for the prevention and treatment of paediatric ASD and PTSD, we reviewed the literature published up to December 2025. Eligible studies included participants aged younger than 18 years and evaluated pharmacological interventions targeting ASD, PTSD prevention or PTSD treatment. After screening and a full-text review, 75 publications were included. Given the methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. Evidence for pharmacological interventions in paediatric trauma-related disorders remains limited and heterogeneous. For PTSD prevention, only limited data support sertraline and, in the context of ASD, imipramine. Limited data also suggest that opioids used for pain management after trauma may reduce subsequent PTSD risk. Early opioid (morphine) exposure for pain management was also associated with lower subsequent severity symptoms in observational paediatric burn studies. Evidence for PTSD treatment is weaker. Anticonvulsants (sodium valproate, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine), antipsychotics (clozapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole), glutamatergics (D-cycloserine, ketamine, ifenprodil), propranolol and cannabidiol do not appear to provide sufficient benefit for routine use. Alpha-adrenergic agents (prazosin, clonidine, guanfacine) have shown preliminary signals of benefit, particularly for hyperarousal and trauma-related sleep disturbances. However, these findings are based on non-randomised and uncontrolled studies. Antidepressants (sertraline, citalopram) show mixed results; among them, citalopram was associated with symptomatic improvement in one small open-label study and one case series. These findings should be considered preliminary and hypothesis generating. No pharmacological treatment has sufficient evidence to warrant routine recommendation for paediatric PTSD and ASD. Pharmacotherapy should therefore be considered only as an adjunct to trauma-focused psychotherapy in selected clinical situations. Further randomised controlled trials are needed.

papers.title: Integrated systems integrating self-care: Supporting the prevention and mitigation of team member burnout and compassion fatigue.
papers.abstract: Health care providers are among the highest risk professionals in Western culture(s) for burnout and compassion fatigue (BO/CF). Although they report being wholly committed to what they do, they are often overwhelmed by the intensity and volume of their clinical responsibilities and patient panels, workplace and interdisciplinary politics, administrative demands, and a tendency to underreport personal struggles or seek help. Trends show, too, that these sequelae are becoming even more prevalent-not less-over recent years. After reviewing literature for this conceptual article across both behavioral/mental health and biomedical/physical health fields, we determined that conventional wisdom regarding the prevention and mitigation of BO/CF-that is, calling for providers to engage in generic self-care practices like sleep hygiene, physical activity, strategic time management, and appropriate boundary-setting-is not enough. Preventing and mitigating burnout and compassion fatigue through multisystemic approaches is superior to monomodal approaches that focus solely on individual self-care practices. This article expands the scope to integrate baseline individual self-care with empirically supported strategies across other system levels (e.g., workplace teams, operational/administrative care structures) designed to synchronously-and holistically-promote provider health and well-being. Purposeful efforts to attend to BO/CF prevention and mitigation across multiple system levels in integrated care contexts are both indicated and essential. Doing so will promote the health and well-being of our providers and facilitate the delivery of high(est) quality care to the patients and families we serve. papers.title: Cross-species multi-omics integration reveals lung alterations in acute kidney injury across mouse, pig, and human airway organoid models
papers.abstract: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequently associated with the development of distant acute lung injury (ALI); however, its broader clinical impact and the underlying temporal molecular mechanics remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We used aggregate deidentified Epic Cosmos data to describe all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay (LOS) in an AKI cohort (13,815,092 patients; 2016-2025) and a subgroup with subsequent lung injury (AKI-lung). Mechanistically, we integrated matched RNA-seq and proteomics from a hyper-acute pig model (4 h reperfusion), an established mouse model (24 h reperfusion), and primary lung organoids exposed to mtDAMP-conditioned media, using MOFA+, PROGENy, decoupleR/CollecTRI, and DIABLO. Candidates were validated in primary human donor lungs obtained from LifeLink, separated into Control (< 1.3 mg/dL, n = 4) and Clinical AKI ([≥] 1.3 mg/dL, n = 3) groups based on admission blood creatinine level. Results: The AKI-lung subgroup had higher observed mortality than the overall AKI cohort (36.67% vs. 25.45%, p < 0.001). Mean hospital LOS was 11.3 versus 6.9 days in the reported AKI-lung and AKI alone queries, respectively (unadjusted p < 0.001). Multi-omics analyses cross-species indicated a temporal shift in proteogenomic coupling. In the hyper-acute pig model, we observed a largely post-translational response (r = -0.06), including ciliary breakdown and metabolic changes associated with PDHA1 protein depletion (Log2FC = -1.53), with minimal transcript level changes. The established mouse model showed a coordinated transcriptional inflammatory response (r = 0.316), characterized by PI3K/Akt pathway activation and downregulation of vascular and immune regulators (Aplnr, Cd74). Human lung organoids exhibited transcriptional downregulation of tissue remodeling genes and persistent ATF6/ATF4-associated ER stress, consistent with a reparative phase under proteostatic strain. Unsupervised MOFA+ revealed conserved cross-species axes (Factors 6 and 7) linked to vascular repair and hemostasis. Upstream regulon analysis identified the endothelial integrity regulators, including FOXF1. Most importantly, targeted validation in primary human donor lungs confirmed a statistically significant, selective down-regulation of the core circadian regulator circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) transcript (p < 0.05), independent of donor age, sex, race. Conclusions: Aggregate clinical findings suggest an association between lung injury following AKI and worse outcome. Kidney-Lung crosstalk initiates as hyper-acute post-translational microvascular breakdown in swine and rapidly transitions into localized uncoupling of cell-autonomous pulmonary circadian machinery (CLOCK) in clinical human AKI, offering human-validated targets to intercept distant organ failure.
